label: eq:X-Phi-commutator
title: Lemma
body_md:
Let \(u\) and \(C\) belong to a Grassmann algebra \(\mathcal{G}\)
generated by a finite number of elements
\(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_s\), \(s>1\), with \(u\) belonging to the even
part of \(\mathcal{G}\) and \(C\) to the odd part of \(\mathcal{G}\).
Assume that \(u\) and \(C\) belong to
\(\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})\), in the sense that every coefficient with
respect to the basis generated by
\(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_s\) belongs to
\(\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})\). Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:X-Phi-commutator}
[\widetilde{X},\Phi]=0.
\end{equation}
head: environment

label: eq:Dx-Phi-commutator
title: Proof
body_md:
We first notice that, besides \(
[D_x,\widetilde{X}]=0,
\) one also has
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Dx-Phi-commutator}
[D_x,\Phi]=0.
\end{equation}
In fact, the same argument which yields
\eqref{eq:Dx-X-commutator} also applies to
\eqref{eq:Dx-Phi-commutator}.

In order to prove the lemma, it is enough to verify
\begin{align}
[\widetilde{X},\Phi]u&=0,
\label{eq:X-Phi-u}\\
[\widetilde{X},\Phi]C&=0.
\label{eq:X-Phi-C}
\end{align}

Let us check \eqref{eq:X-Phi-u}. We have
\[
\widetilde{X}u=K[u],
\qquad
\Phi u=P[u]C.
\]
Then, using \eqref{eq:Dx-X-commutator}, we get
\begin{align}
\widetilde{X}\Phi u
&=
D_x^3\widetilde{X}C
+
u_x\widetilde{X}C
+
2D_xC\cdot\widetilde{X}u
+
2uD_x\widetilde{X}C
\nonumber\\
&=
D_x^3\mathcal{Y}[u,C]
+
\bigl(D_x^4u+D_x(3uu_x)\bigr)C
+
u_x\bigl(C_{xxx}+3uC_x\bigr)
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
2\bigl(u_{xxx}+3uu_x\bigr)C_x
+
2u\bigl(C_{xxxx}+3u_xC_x+3uC_{xx}\bigr).
\label{eq:X-Phi-u-first}
\end{align}
On the other hand,
\begin{align}
\Phi\widetilde{X}u
&=
D_x^3\mathcal{Y}
+
D_x^4u\cdot C
+
u_xD_x^3C
+
3D_x^3u\cdot D_xC
+
3D_x^2u\cdot D_x^2C
\nonumber\\
&\quad
-
\Bigl(
D_x^3u\cdot D_xC
+
3D_x^2u\cdot D_x^2C
+
3D_xu\cdot D_x^3C
+
uD_x^4C
\Bigr)
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
3\bigl(D_x^3C+CD_xu+2uD_xC\bigr)D_xu
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
3uD_x\bigl(D_x^3C+CD_xu+2uD_xC\bigr).
\label{eq:Phi-X-u}
\end{align}

Finally, comparing each coefficient of the \(x\)-derivatives of \(C\),
we obtain (8). A similar calculation yields
\eqref{eq:X-Phi-C}.

The lemma implies that the BRST transformation maps solutions into
solutions of the KdV--ghost system.
head: environment

label: PL1
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Nilpotent gauge conjugation

title: Proof
body_md:
From the explicit form of \(G\),
\[
G^{-1}D_xG
=
D_x+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}C_x.
\]
Therefore,
\[
G^{-1}D_x^2G
=
D_x^2+\varepsilon C_xD_x
+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}C_{xx},
\]
and hence
\[
G^{-1}\mathscr{L}_0G
=
D_x^2+\varepsilon C_xD_x
+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}C_{xx}
+\frac12 uI
=
\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}
\]

Similarly,
\[
G^{-1}D_x^3G
=
D_x^3
+\frac{3\varepsilon}{2}C_xD_x^2
+\frac{3\varepsilon}{2}C_{xx}D_x
+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}C_{xxx}.
\]

Using the explicit form of $\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}$ given in (15), the
previous identity yields
\[
G^{-1}\mathcal{M}_0G
=
\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}
+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
\left(C_{xxx}+3uC_x\right)I.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}
=
G^{-1}\mathcal{M}_0G
-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
\left(C_{xxx}+3uC_x\right)I.
\]

Using also
\[
G^{-1}G_t=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}C_t,
\]
direct substitution gives
\[
G^{-1}\mathscr{M}_0G-G^{-1}G_t
=
\mathscr{M}_{\varepsilon}
-
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\Theta[u,C]\,I.
\]

On solutions of the ghost equation, $\Theta[u,C]=0$, and the usual temporal
gauge relation is recovered. Under this assumption, the extended Lax equation
(16) reduces, through the gauge transformation (19)--(20), to the standard
KdV Lax equation.
head: environment

label: teo1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{teo1}                  
Under the assumptions above, the resolvent sets of $\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}$ and $\mathscr{L}_{0}$ satisfy
\[
\rho(\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon})
=
\rho(\mathscr{L}_0).
\]
Consequently, their spectra satisfy
\[
\sigma(\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon})
=
\sigma(\mathscr{L}_0).
\]
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In fact, the spectra of $\mathscr{L}_\varepsilon$ and $\mathscr{L}_0$ are defined by
\[
\sigma(\mathscr{L}_\varepsilon)
=
\Lambda_0\setminus\rho(\mathscr{L}_\varepsilon),
\]
and
\[
\sigma(\mathscr{L}_0)
=
\Lambda_0\setminus\rho(\mathscr{L}_0),
\]
respectively. Therefore,
\[
\sigma(\mathscr{L}_\varepsilon)
=
\sigma(\mathscr{L}_0).
\]
That is, the spectra of $\mathscr{L}_\varepsilon$ and
$\mathscr{L}_0$, both with domain
$H^2(\mathbb{R})\otimes\Lambda$, coincide.
Notice that the elements of the spectrum belong to $\Lambda_0$.

The resolvent set of $\mathscr{L}_\varepsilon$ is the set of
$\lambda\in\Lambda_0$ such that
\[
\mathscr{L}_\varepsilon-\lambda I:
H^2(\mathbb{R})\otimes\Lambda
\longrightarrow
L^2(\mathbb{R})\otimes\Lambda
\]
is bijective and its inverse is bounded.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have
\[
\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}-\lambda I
=
G^{-1}
(\mathscr{L}_0-\lambda I)G,
\]
hence
\[
(\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}-\lambda I)^{-1}
=
G^{-1}
(\mathscr{L}_0-\lambda I)^{-1}G.
\]

Consequently, the inverse of one operator exists if and only if the inverse
of the other operator exists. Moreover, one operator is bounded if and only
if the other one is also bounded. This is so, under the assumption that the
Grassmann algebra valued fields $u$ and $C$ belong to the Schwartz space.
In fact, G is bounded and the product of $G$ with elements of the Hilbert space $L^2$ or $H^2$
also belongs to $L^2$ or $H^2$ respectively. We then have
\[
\rho(\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon})
=
\rho(\mathscr{L}_0),
\]
which implies
\[
\sigma(\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon})
=
\sigma(\mathscr{L}_0).
\]
head: environment

label: lem2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem2}
The following holds:
\[
\sigma_B(\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}) = \sigma_B(\mathscr{L}_0) = \sigma(\mathscr{L}_{0B})
\]
                                                                             

where
\(
\mathscr{L}_{0B}
=
D_x^2+\frac{1}{2}u_BI
\)
is the body operator on \(L^2(\mathbb{R})\), with domain
\(H^2(\mathbb{R})\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\lambda\in\Lambda_0$ and decompose $\lambda$ and $u$ into their body
and soul parts as
\[
\lambda=\lambda_B+\lambda_S,\qquad
u=u_B+u_S.
\]
If $\lambda_B\in\rho(\mathcal L_{0B})$, then
\[
\mathscr{L}_0 - \lambda I = \Big(\mathscr{L}_{0B} - \lambda_B I \Big)\Bigg[ I - \Big(\mathscr{L}_{0B} - \lambda_B I \Big)^{-1} \left(\lambda_S - \dfrac{1}{2}u_S \right)  \Bigg]
\]
where $\ (\mathscr{L}_{0B} - \lambda_B I)^{-1}\left(\lambda_S - \dfrac{1}{2}u_S \right)$ is nilpotent. Thus $I - (\mathscr{L}_{0B} - \lambda_B I)^{-1} \left(\lambda_S - \dfrac{1}{2}u_S \right)$
is invertible. Consequently, if $\lambda_B\in\rho(\mathcal{L}_{0B})$, then, for every
nilpotent $\lambda_S$, the element $\lambda=\lambda_B+\lambda_S$ belongs to
$\rho(\mathcal{L}_0)$. Conversely, if $\lambda\in\rho(\mathcal{L}_0)$, then
its body $\lambda_B$ belongs to $\rho(\mathcal{L}_{0B})$. Therefore,
\[
\rho_B(\mathcal{L}_0)=\rho(\mathcal{L}_{0B}),
\]
and hence
\[
\sigma_B(\mathcal{L}_0)=\sigma(\mathcal{L}_{0B}).
\]
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $\hat{\lambda}$ be an isolated eigenvalue of $\mathscr{L}_{0B}$ and $P$ the spectral projection from $H^2 (\mathbb{R}) \otimes \Lambda$ to the space of eigenfunctions with eigenvalue $\hat{\lambda}$.

Let $\lambda \in \Lambda_0$ be an eigenvalue of $\mathscr{L}_0$ with body $\hat{\lambda}$:
\[
\mathscr{L}_0 \psi = \lambda \psi = (\hat{\lambda} + \lambda_S)\psi ,
\]
and assume $u_S=0$. Then, if the body of $P\psi \neq 0$, $\lambda_S = 0$.

In fact,
\[
P \mathscr{L}_0 \psi = \mathscr{L}_0 P \psi = \hat{\lambda} P \psi,
\]
then
\[
(\hat{\lambda} + \lambda_S) P \psi = \mathscr{L}_0 P \psi = \hat{\lambda} P \psi
\]

which implies $\lambda_S P \psi = 0$. Consequently,
\[
\lambda_S = 0 .
\]

                                                                                     
Consequently, if $u_S=0$ and the body of $P\psi \neq 0$, where $\psi$ is an eigenfunction
of $\mathscr{L}_0$, then the associated eigenvalue has no soul and
it is the real eigenvalue of $\mathscr{L}_{0B}$.
head: environment

label: thm:triangular-zcr
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:triangular-zcr}
Let $U$ and $V$ be the matrices appearing in (29) and defined by
(30)--(33), and let $v=C_x$.
Then the zero-curvature condition \eqref{eq:zero-curvature} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{RL=0}
\mathcal{R}[u]=0,
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_u[v]=0.
\end{equation}
Hence the triangular zero-curvature condition is equivalent to the
local KdV--ghost system.
head: environment
name: Triangular zero-curvature representation

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:curvature-block-form}, the zero-curvature condition is
equivalent to \(
Z_0=0,
\quad
Z_1=0.
\) Equation~\eqref{eq:Z0-residue} shows that
\(
Z_0=0 \) if and only if \(
\mathcal{R}[u]=0.
\) Likewise, from \eqref{eq:Z1-local},
\(
Z_1=0 \) if and only if \(
\mathcal{L}_u[v]=0,
\)
because the lower-right entry of \(Z_1\) is
\(-\mathcal{L}_u[v]\).
Therefore the zero-curvature condition is equivalent to \eqref{RL=0}
which is precisely the local KdV--ghost system.
head: environment

label: prop:factorization-identities
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Factorization identities

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the two bosonic identities. From
\[
u=2\alpha-2p^2-2p_x,
\]
we obtain
\[
u_t=
-4pp_t-2p_{xt}, \qquad
u_x
=
-4pp_x-2p_{xx}, \qquad
u_{xxx}
=
-12p_xp_{xx}-4pp_{xxx}-2p_{xxxx}.
\]

Substitution into
\(
\mathcal{R}[u]
\)
and collection of terms gives
\[
\mathcal{R}[u]
=
-2\partial_x E_p-4pE_p
=
-2(D_x+2p)E_p,
\]
which proves~\eqref{eq:factorization-R-u}.

Similarly, substituting
\[
\widetilde{u}
=
2\alpha-2p^2+2p_x
\]
into the KdV residue gives
\[
\mathcal{R}[\widetilde{u}]
=
2\left(D_x-2p\right)E_p,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:factorization-R-utilde}. Equivalently, this
second identity follows from the first one under the involution
\(
p\longmapsto -p.
\) Indeed, under \(p\mapsto -p\) one has
\(u\mapsto\widetilde u\) and \(E_p\mapsto -E_p\).

We now derive the ghost identities by nilpotent linearization. Let
\(
p_{\varepsilon}
=
p+\varepsilon\eta,
\quad
\varepsilon^2=0,
\)
where \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\) are odd, so that
\(p_{\varepsilon}\) is even. The corresponding fields satisfy
\begin{align*}
u_{\varepsilon}
&=
2\alpha-2p_{\varepsilon}^2
-2(p_{\varepsilon})_x
=
u+\varepsilon v,
\\
\widetilde{u}_{\varepsilon}
&=
2\alpha-2p_{\varepsilon}^2
+2(p_{\varepsilon})_x
=
\widetilde{u}
+\varepsilon\widetilde{v}.
\end{align*}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Ep-nilpotent-expansion}
E_{p_{\varepsilon}}
=
E_p+\varepsilon E_{\eta}.
\end{equation}

Since \(p_\varepsilon\) is even, the algebraic identity~(52a)
applies to \(p_\varepsilon\). In fact,
\[
\mathcal{R}[u_{\varepsilon}]
=
-2
\left(
D_x+2p_{\varepsilon}
\right)
E_{p_{\varepsilon}}.
\]
Using \(
\mathcal{R}[u+\varepsilon v]
=
\mathcal{R}[u]
+\varepsilon\mathcal{L}_u[v]
\) and \eqref{eq:Ep-nilpotent-expansion}, the coefficient of
\(\varepsilon\) yields
\[
\mathcal{L}_u[v]
=
-2\left[
\left(D_x+2p\right)E_{\eta}
+2\eta E_p
\right].
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:factorization-L-u}.

Likewise, applying \eqref{eq:factorization-R-utilde} to
\(p_{\varepsilon}\) gives
\[
\mathcal{R}[\widetilde{u}_{\varepsilon}]
=
2
\left(
D_x-2p_{\varepsilon}
\right)
E_{p_{\varepsilon}}.
\]
Taking the coefficient of \(\varepsilon\), we obtain
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\widetilde{u}}[\widetilde{v}]
=
2\left[
\left(D_x-2p\right)E_{\eta}
-2\eta E_p
\right],
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:factorization-L-utilde}.
head: environment

label: lem:auxiliary-compatibility
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Compatibility of the auxiliary ghost system

label: eq:b-functional
title: Proof
body_md:
Introduce the functions
\begin{align*}
a[u,p]
&:=
\alpha-\frac{1}{2}u-p^2, \qquad
b[u,p]:=
-\frac{1}{2}u_x+(4\alpha+u)p.
\label{eq:b-functional}
\end{align*}
Then the auxiliary equations for \(p\) can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\label{eq:p-system-ab}
p_x=a[u,p],
\qquad
p_t=D_xb[u,p].
\end{equation*}

Using the auxiliary equations for \(p\), a direct calculation gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:p-compatibility-residue}
\partial_t a[u,p]
-
D_x^2 b[u,p]
=
-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}[u].
\end{equation}
Indeed,
\begin{align*}
\partial_t a[u,p]
-
D_x^2 b[u,p]
&=
-\frac{1}{2}u_t
-2pp_t
+\frac{1}{2}u_{xxx}
-u_{xx}p
-2u_xp_x
-(4\alpha+u)p_{xx}.
\end{align*}
From the auxiliary system,
\[
p_t
=
-\frac{1}{2}u_{xx}
+u_xp
+(4\alpha+u)p_x,
\]
whereas differentiation of the spatial Riccati equation gives
\[
p_{xx}
=
-\frac{1}{2}u_x
-2pp_x.
\]
Substitution of these expressions yields
\[
\partial_t a[u,p]
-
D_x^2 b[u,p]
=
-\frac{1}{2}
\left(
u_t-u_{xxx}-3uu_x
\right)
=
-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}[u].
\]

Consequently, the compatibility of the auxiliary system for \(p\)
follows from \(\mathcal{R}[u]=0\).

Consider now the nilpotent deformation
\(
u_{\varepsilon}
=
u+\varepsilon v,
\quad
p_{\varepsilon}
=
p+\varepsilon\eta,
\quad
\varepsilon^2=0.
\)
The Fréchet derivatives of \(a\) and \(b\) in the direction
\((v,\eta)\) are
\begin{align*}
D a[u,p](v,\eta)
&=
-\frac{1}{2}v-2p\eta,
\\
D b[u,p](v,\eta)
&=
-\frac{1}{2}v_x
+vp
+(4\alpha+u)\eta.
\end{align*}
Thus,
\[
\eta_x
=
D a[u,p](v,\eta),
\qquad
\eta_t
=
D_xD b[u,p](v,\eta).
\]

Taking the Fréchet derivative of
\eqref{eq:p-compatibility-residue} in the direction \((v,\eta)\)
gives
\[
\partial_t
\left(
D a[u,p](v,\eta)
\right)
-
D_x^2
\left(
D b[u,p](v,\eta)
\right)
=
-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_u[v].
\]
Using the auxiliary equations for \(\eta\), this becomes
\[
\partial_t(\eta_x)
-
D_x(\eta_t)
=
-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_u[v].
\]
Since the seed fields satisfy
\(
\mathcal{L}_u[v]=0,
\)
we conclude that
\(
\partial_t(\eta_x)
=
\partial_x(\eta_t).
\)
Finally, let \(\eta_1\) and \(\eta_2\) be two solutions of
\eqref{eq:eta-auxiliary-system}. Subtracting their spatial
equations gives
\[
(\eta_1-\eta_2)_x
=
-2p(\eta_1-\eta_2),
\]
whereas subtracting their temporal equations gives
\[
(\eta_1-\eta_2)_t
=
\left[
(4\alpha+u)(\eta_1-\eta_2)
\right]_x.
\]
Therefore, setting
\(
\rho:=\eta_1-\eta_2,
\)
we obtain
\[
\rho_x=-2p\rho,
\qquad
\rho_t=
\left[
(4\alpha+u)\rho
\right]_x,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:eta-homogeneous-system}.
head: environment

label: thm:nilpotent-darboux-transformation
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:nilpotent-darboux-transformation}
Let \((u,v)\) be a sufficiently smooth solution of the local
KdV--ghost system \eqref{eq:local-system-residue}. Fix an even parameter \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\). Suppose that the even
field \(p\) and the odd field \(\eta\) satisfy
\begin{subequations}
\label{eq:auxiliary-system-darboux-theorem}
\begin{align}
p_x
&=
\alpha-\frac{1}{2}u-p^2,
\label{eq:p-spatial-darboux-theorem}
\\
p_t
&=
\left[
-\frac{1}{2}u_x+(4\alpha+u)p
\right]_x,
\label{eq:p-temporal-darboux-theorem}
\\
\eta_x
&=
-\frac{1}{2}v-2p\eta,
\label{eq:eta-spatial-darboux-theorem}
\\
\eta_t
&=
\left[
-\frac{1}{2}v_x+vp+(4\alpha+u)\eta
\right]_x.
\label{eq:eta-temporal-darboux-theorem}
\end{align}
\end{subequations}

Define \((\widetilde u,\widetilde v)\) by~\eqref{eq:nilpotent-darboux-fields}. Then the transformed
pair also satisfies the local KdV--ghost system: \( \mathcal{R}[\widetilde{u}]
=
0,
\quad
\mathcal{L}_{\widetilde{u}}[\widetilde{v}]
=
0.
\)
head: environment
name: Nilpotent Darboux transformation

title: Proof
body_md:
The auxiliary equations for \(p\) and \(\eta\) imply \(
E_p=0,
\quad
E_{\eta}=0.
\)
The factorization identities of
Proposition~\ref{prop:factorization-identities} therefore give
\[
\mathcal{R}[\widetilde{u}]
=
2(D_x-2p)E_p
=
0
\]
and
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\widetilde{u}}[\widetilde{v}]
=
2\left[
(D_x-2p)E_{\eta}-2\eta E_p
\right]
=
0.
\]
Hence \((\widetilde{u},\widetilde{v})\) satisfies the local
KdV--ghost system.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let
\[
u^{[0]}\longrightarrow u^{[1]}\longrightarrow\cdots
\longrightarrow u^{[n]}
\]
be the bosonic Darboux chain constructed above, with
\[
p^{[j]}=(\log\phi_j)_x,
\qquad
u^{[j]}=u^{[j-1]}+4p^{[j]}_x,
\qquad
\alpha_j=\kappa_j^2.
\]
Fix $j\geq 1$ and work on a domain on which $\phi_j\neq 0$. Assume that
\(
\bigl(u^{[j-1]},v^{[j-1]}\bigr)
\)
satisfies the local KdV--ghost system, and let
$\eta^{[j]}_p$ be a particular solution of
\[
(\eta^{[j]}_p)_x
=
-\frac12 v^{[j-1]}
-2p^{[j]}\eta^{[j]}_p,\qquad
(\eta^{[j]}_p)_t
=
\left[
-\frac12(v^{[j-1]})_x
+p^{[j]}v^{[j-1]}
+\left(4\kappa_j^2+u^{[j-1]}\right)
\eta^{[j]}_p
\right]_x.
\]

Then every solution of the corresponding auxiliary ghost system is of
the form
\[
\eta^{[j]}
=
\eta^{[j]}_p+\zeta_j\phi_j^{-2},
\]
where $\zeta_j$ is an odd element of the underlying Grassmann algebra
independent of $x$ and $t$.

Defining
\[
v^{[j]}
=
v^{[j-1]}+4(\eta^{[j]})_x,
\]
the pair
\(
\bigl(u^{[j]},v^{[j]}\bigr)
\)
again satisfies the local KdV--ghost system.

Consequently, starting from $v^{[0]}=0$, the Darboux chain can be
lifted recursively to the ghost sector, yielding
\(
v^{[j]}
=
v^{[j]}(x,t;\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_j),
\quad
j=1,\ldots,n,
\)
with one new odd homogeneous parameter introduced at each Darboux step.
head: environment
name: Recursive ghost extension of the Darboux chain

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $j\geq 1$ and work on a domain on which $\phi_j\neq 0$. By construction,
\[
p^{[j]}=(\log\phi_j)_x=\frac{(\phi_j)_x}{\phi_j},
\]
and $\phi_j$ satisfies the complete scalar Lax pair on the
background $u^{[j-1]}$ at the spectral value $\kappa_j^2$:
\[
(\phi_j)_{xx}
=
\left(
\kappa_j^2-\frac12u^{[j-1]}
\right)\phi_j,\qquad (\phi_j)_t
=
-\frac12(u^{[j-1]})_x\phi_j
+
\left(
4\kappa_j^2+u^{[j-1]}
\right)(\phi_j)_x.
\]
It follows that
\[
p^{[j]}_x
=
\kappa_j^2-\frac12u^{[j-1]}-(p^{[j]})^2,
\]
and, since $p^{[j]}=(\log\phi_j)_x$,
\[
p^{[j]}_t
=
\left[
-\frac12(u^{[j-1]})_x
+
\left(
4\kappa_j^2+u^{[j-1]}
\right)p^{[j]}
\right]_x.
\]
Thus $p^{[j]}$ satisfies the bosonic auxiliary system of
Theorem~3 with $\alpha=\kappa_j^2$.

Now assume that
\(
\bigl(u^{[j-1]},v^{[j-1]}\bigr)
\)
satisfies the local KdV--ghost system. By Lemma~3, the
corresponding auxiliary ghost system is compatible. Let
$\eta_p^{[j]}$ be a particular solution and let $\eta^{[j]}$
be any other solution. Setting
\(
\rho:=\eta^{[j]}-\eta_p^{[j]},
\)
the difference satisfies the homogeneous system
\[
\rho_x=-2p^{[j]}\rho,
\qquad
\rho_t=
\left[
\left(
4\kappa_j^2+u^{[j-1]}
\right)\rho
\right]_x.
\]

Using
\[
p^{[j]}=\frac{(\phi_j)_x}{\phi_j},
\]
the spatial equation gives
\[
(\phi_j^2\rho)_x
=
2\phi_j(\phi_j)_x\rho+\phi_j^2\rho_x
=
0.
\]
Let
\[
A_j:=4\kappa_j^2+u^{[j-1]}.
\]
From
\[
(\phi_j)_t
=
-\frac12(u^{[j-1]})_x\phi_j
+
A_j(\phi_j)_x,
\]
together with
\[
\rho_t=(A_j\rho)_x,
\qquad
(A_j)_x=(u^{[j-1]})_x,
\]
we also obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\phi_j^2\rho)_t
&=
2\phi_j(\phi_j)_t\rho+\phi_j^2\rho_t
\\
&=
2\phi_j
\left[
-\frac12(u^{[j-1]})_x\phi_j
+
A_j(\phi_j)_x
\right]\rho
\\
&\quad
+
\phi_j^2
\left[
(u^{[j-1]})_x\rho+A_j\rho_x
\right]
\\
&=0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where in the last step we used
\[
\rho_x=-2p^{[j]}\rho
=
-2\frac{(\phi_j)_x}{\phi_j}\rho.
\]
Hence $\phi_j^2\rho$ is independent of both $x$ and $t$.

 Denoting this
odd constant by $\zeta_j$, we obtain
\[
\eta^{[j]}
=
\eta_p^{[j]}+\zeta_j\phi_j^{-2}.
\]

We now define
\[
v^{[j]}
=
v^{[j-1]}+4(\eta^{[j]})_x.
\]
The fields $p^{[j]}$ and $\eta^{[j]}$ satisfy the bosonic and
ghost auxiliary equations of Theorem~3, respectively, with
$\alpha=\kappa_j^2$. Therefore Theorem~3 gives
\[
u^{[j]}
=
u^{[j-1]}+4p^{[j]}_x,
\qquad
v^{[j]}
=
v^{[j-1]}+4(\eta^{[j]})_x,
\]
and guarantees that
\(
\bigl(u^{[j]},v^{[j]}\bigr)
\)
again satisfies the local KdV--ghost system.

For the initial step, $v^{[0]}=0$, and one may choose
\(
\eta_p^{[1]}=0.
\)
Hence
\[
\eta^{[1]}=\zeta_1\phi_1^{-2},
\qquad
v^{[1]}=4\zeta_1(\phi_1^{-2})_x.
\]
The preceding argument then provides the inductive step
\[
\bigl(u^{[j-1]},v^{[j-1]}\bigr)
\longmapsto
\bigl(u^{[j]},v^{[j]}\bigr),
\]
so the construction can be repeated for
$j=1,\ldots,n$.

Finally, the resulting family does not depend on the choice of
particular solution. Indeed, if $\widehat\eta_p^{[j]}$ is another
particular solution, then
\[
\widehat\eta_p^{[j]}-\eta_p^{[j]}
=
c\,\phi_j^{-2}
\]
for some $x$- and $t$-independent odd constant $c$. Hence
\[
\eta_p^{[j]}+\zeta_j\phi_j^{-2}
=
\widehat\eta_p^{[j]}
+
(\zeta_j-c)\phi_j^{-2},
\]
so changing the particular solution only redefines the homogeneous
parameter $\zeta_j$.
